idea: A load-cell parts bin that weighs its contents and alerts when stock runs low
target_customer: Parts departments at franchised car dealerships

found.text: NADA counts 16,991 franchised light-vehicle dealers in the US (mid-year 2026).
In the first half of 2026, dealerships wrote more than 136 million repair orders, with service and parts sales of nearly $83 billion.
Weight-based bins that trigger restocks already exist from industrial suppliers: Fastenal's scale FASTBin restocks when quantity falls below the item's min level.
eTurns SensorBins hardware costs around $96 per item, on top of the Optimize plan subscription.
A dealer consultant describes min/max levels in the business management software that tell staff when it is time to reorder.
The same consultant writes that non-parts people entering the parts department are generally the reason counts are off.
The existing weight-bin products found are sold into manufacturing and MRO, not dealership parts departments, so a dealership-focused version could be an open niche.
Because the dealer management system already flags reorder points, the bin's value would come from catching miscounts (shrink, unrecorded pulls), not from the alert itself.

unknowns: How many bins or fast-moving part numbers a typical dealership parts department would put on scales.
Whether the parts manager, fixed-ops director, or dealer principal approves a purchase like this.
Whether the bins must integrate with the dealer management system (CDK, Reynolds, etc.) to be useful, and whether those vendors allow it.
How often dealership parts departments actually run out of fast-moving bin parts, and what a stockout costs them.
Public pricing for Fastenal FASTBin scales, SupplyPro SmartBin, and TeDaLoS sensors (none found).
The consultant article cited is written for outdoor power equipment dealers; no car-dealership-specific source on bin-level inventory practice was read.

riskiest_assumptions.assumption: Dealership parts departments lose meaningful money or time to stockouts of small bin parts that a scale would catch.
riskiest_assumptions.why_risky: The DMS already flags reorder points; if counts are mostly accurate, the bin adds little. No dealership-specific stockout data was found.
riskiest_assumptions.how_to_test: Ask five parts managers to walk through the last time a bin part ran out unexpectedly, and what it cost (lost RO time, emergency order, freight).

riskiest_assumptions.assumption: A parts manager will pay about $80 per bin without needing DMS integration.
riskiest_assumptions.why_risky: Alerts that don't update the DMS on-hand count may be seen as one more screen to watch; integration may be required and hard to get.
riskiest_assumptions.how_to_test: Ask parts managers how they acted on the last reorder alert they received and which system it came from.

riskiest_assumptions.assumption: Dealerships would buy from a new hardware vendor rather than from Fastenal, Würth, or an OEM-endorsed supplier they already use.
riskiest_assumptions.why_risky: Industrial distributors bundle bins with supply contracts; dealers may get similar tech free with a consumables program.
riskiest_assumptions.how_to_test: Ask who supplies their shop consumables today and whether that supplier has ever offered managed bins.

riskiest_assumptions.assumption: A typical dealership would put around 50 bins on scales.
riskiest_assumptions.why_risky: This number drives the market size; it is a pure guess.
riskiest_assumptions.how_to_test: Ask parts managers to count how many part numbers they would describe as fast-moving small parts kept in open bins.

interview_script.intro: Thanks for your time. I'm learning how dealership parts departments keep track of small, fast-moving parts. I'm not selling anything today.

questions.question: Tell me about the last time a part you normally stock ran out before you noticed.
questions.listening_for: Which parts, how it was discovered, what it cost (tech downtime, emergency order, freight, lost sale).

questions.question: How do you decide when to reorder small bin parts today?
questions.listening_for: DMS min/max, visual checks, distributor reps, subscriptions; how much manual work it takes.

questions.question: Walk me through your last cycle count. What did you find?
questions.listening_for: How far off counts were, causes (techs pulling parts, unrecorded usage), time spent.

questions.question: Who supplies your shop consumables and fasteners today, and how does restocking work with them?
questions.listening_for: Fastenal, Würth, OEM programs, vendor-managed bins; whether a supplier already restocks for them.

questions.question: What have you tried in the past to keep better track of parts on the shelf?
questions.listening_for: Past tools or processes, why they stuck or were dropped, who approved the spend.

questions.question: When you last bought equipment or software for the parts department, who signed off and how long did it take?
questions.listening_for: Decision maker, budget size, approval process.

description.text: Scale-based bins that trigger a restock when quantity falls below the item's min level, alerting the local Fastenal branch.

price.text: No public price found; bins appear to be bundled with a Fastenal supply program.

description.text: Weight sensors under bins work with TrackStock IoT cloud software for automated replenishment.

price.text: Hardware around $96 per item, available to Optimize Plan customers at an additional hardware cost.

description.text: A cabinet storage system with weight-based sensing and a standard RFID badge reader to identify employee access.
Sensor units continuously measure the content weight of the container and are wireless and fully mobile.

competitors.name: Status quo: DMS min/max plus supplier subscriptions

description.text: Business management software alerts staff when a part reaches its minimum level; Würth USA offers automatic weekly or monthly reorders of frequently used products.

price.text: Included in software and supply contracts dealerships already pay for, so no extra cost.

market_size.price_covers: The one-time hardware price per bin only. Any subscription or service fee is left out. purchases_per_year spreads that one-time price over the bin's replacement cycle.

customers.unit: franchised light-vehicle dealers in the US

purchases_per_year.unit: bin replacements per year (one every 3-5 years)

sam_share.unit: fraction of dealerships that could buy

som_share.unit: fraction of SAM we could win in 3 years
